notes.title: Chapter map: Memory management & GC
notes.html:
Three ways memory leaves a Python process, and one note on finding out which one failed. Read each arrow as a sentence: the cyclic GC built on reference counting.

Green = CORE, blue = SUPPORTING, grey = another chapter (dashed edges).

Reading order:28 reference counting29 cyclic GC30 weakrefs31 allocators32 diagnosing memory
  • The one big idea: freeing is three separate events. Refcounting frees an object the instant its last reference goes (28); the cyclic GC frees what refcounting can't, namely cycles (29); and the allocator gives memory back to the OS only in whole empty arenas (31). "RSS didn't drop" can be any of the three, which is what 32 untangles.
  • The two most-confused pairs: object freed vs memory returned to the OS (28 vs 31: a freed object's block stays in Python's arena) · weakref vs strong reference (30: a weak reference finds an object without keeping it alive).
  • Ten minutes before an interview: the pictures in 28 (the stored-exception chain) and 29 (only-internal references), then 32's triage flowchart.
  • Cross-chapter: object header (where the count lives) · functools caches (strong references that pin objects: the classic growth a diff finds) · the GIL (unsynchronised refcounts are why it exists).

No decision tree: memory diagnosis is a flow that belongs to note 32 (symptom → cause), not a choice between these notes.

notes.title: Reference Counting
notes.html:
References

C API: reference counting · sys.getrefcount · CPython InternalDocs: garbage collector design · 📜 PEP 683: Immortal objects · rushter: Garbage collection in Python

TL;DR

Every reference to an object is counted; when the count hits zero, CPython frees it on that line. So freeing is immediate and predictable, and anything still pointing at an object, however indirectly, keeps it alive.

Flow:every new reference (name, slot, argument, frame)Py_INCREFevery dropped onePy_DECREFhits 0? deallocate on that instruction, __del__ firstdecref what it held, which may cascadenever 0 because of a cycle? the cyclic GC's job

Recall

Prompt Answer
When is an object freed in CPython? The moment its refcount reaches 0, inside the instruction that dropped the last ref.
Draw by hand: why big outlives fetch last_error → exception → __traceback__ → frame → locals → big: every arrow is a reference.
What does del x do? Unbinds the name and decrements; frees only if that was the last ref.
How does a stored exception keep data alive? Exception → traceback → frames → their locals.
What can't refcounting free? Cycles: counts never reach 0, so the cyclic GC handles them.
What did PEP 683 change? Core objects are immortal: a fixed count that's never written.

The idea

Garbage-collected languages usually free memory "some time later". Put a print in __del__ and watch when CPython does it:

class Node:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def __del__(self): print(f"  freed {self.name}")

a = Node("solo")                                      # ① a name: INCREF
print("before del"); del a; print("after del")     # ② ③ → before del · freed solo · after del

def fetch():
    big = Node("payload")
    raise ConnectionError("timeout")
try:
    fetch()
except ConnectionError as e:
    last_error = e                  # keep it for a log line later
print("handled"); del last_error    # → handled · freed payload

The first object was freed between the two prints, the instant its last reference went. The second outlived fetch until last_error was deleted: the exception holds its traceback, the traceback holds fetch's frame, and the frame holds big.

The trade: immediate, predictable freeing by counting references on every operation, paid for in constant bookkeeping and in the rule that any path to an object keeps it alive.

How it works

Increments and decrements happen on almost every bytecode instruction; zero triggers deallocation on the spot:

How the count moves for one object, o = O() (CPython 3.12; getrefcount adds one for its own argument):

Step Code sys.getrefcount(o) Why
1 o = O() 2 the name, plus the call's argument
2 l = [o, o] 4 one per list slot
3 d = {"k": o} 5 a dict value is a reference
4 del l 3 the list dies and decrefs both slots
Rule What actually happens
Every reference counts, not just names ob_refcnt rises for each binding, container slot, argument on the stack, attribute, closure cell, and each frame or traceback holding the object (the object header).
del removes a reference, not an object At zero the deallocator runs inside that instruction: __del__, then decrefs of everything the object referenced, which can cascade. A "trashcan" defers very deep cascades so a million-deep nested list frees without overflowing the C stack.
Some references are easy to forget Tracebacks hold frames and locals (the picture); closures hold cells; bound methods hold their instance; lru_cache holds its arguments; module globals live until unload.
The cost, and immortal objects Refcount writes cost CPU, explain the GIL, and un-share forked workers' memory: merely reading an object in a child writes its count and copies the page. PEP 683 (3.12) pins None, small ints and other core objects; free-threaded 3.13+ splits counts.

Code

Keep errors without keeping their data, and drop big intermediates early:

import traceback

def with_retries(call, attempts=3):
    last_exc = None
    for _ in range(attempts):
        try:
            return call()
        except ConnectionError as exc:
            traceback.clear_frames(exc.__traceback__)   # drop frames' locals, keep type + message
            last_exc = exc
    raise RuntimeError(f"gave up after {attempts} attempts") from last_exc

def process_batch(rows):
    parsed = [parse(r) for r in rows]      # large intermediate
    totals = aggregate(parsed)
    del parsed                             # last reference → freed here, before the slow step
    return publish(totals)

del parsed lowers the peak only because it removes the last reference; if parsed were also on self, it would do nothing.

Break it: keep the errors "for a report".

class Payload:
    def __init__(self, i): self.i = i
    def __del__(self): print(f"  freed payload {self.i}")
def fetch(i):
    data = Payload(i)
    raise TimeoutError(f"attempt {i}")
errors = []
for i in range(3):
    try: fetch(i)
    except TimeoutError as exc: errors.append(exc)
print("loop finished"); errors.clear(); print("errors cleared")
# look for: no "freed" lines until errors.clear()
# naive model predicts: each payload freed when its fetch() ended

On CPython 3.12.13: loop finished, then freed payload 2, 1, 0, then errors cleared. Each stored exception pinned a frame and its data; in a service that's how memory grows with the error rate.

Interview

30-second answer: CPython keeps a count of references on every object, incremented for each binding, container slot, argument or frame that points at it, and decremented when one goes away. When it hits zero the object is freed immediately, its own references are released, and memory returns to the allocator. That makes freeing deterministic, but it can't free cycles, which is the cyclic collector's job, and any forgotten reference, like a stored traceback, keeps things alive.

Q · Mechanism — Walk through b = a, del a, del b, and what "freed" actually does. b = a copies the pointer and increments the count. del a unbinds the name and decrements; the object survives because of b. del b decrements to zero, so inside that instruction CPython calls tp_dealloc: __del__ if defined, then decrements of everything this object referenced, possibly cascading, then the memory goes back to pymalloc (#31), not necessarily to the OS. On 3.12, immortal objects like None never reach zero.

Q · Failure — A worker's memory grows in proportion to its error rate, though errors are "handled". Diagnose. Something stores exceptions: a list of recent errors, a retry wrapper's last_exc, a metrics label, a logger with a captured traceback. Each exception holds its traceback, which holds every frame it passed through and all their locals: request bodies, result sets (see Break it). Tests have few errors, so nothing shows. Find it with tracemalloc snapshots grouped by traceback, or gc.get_referrers on a sample payload. Fix: store str(exc) or type(exc), or traceback.clear_frames before keeping it.

Q · Design — A pre-fork server (gunicorn workers) loads a large model or lookup table before forking, and each worker's RSS climbs toward a full copy. Why, and what do you do? Copy-on-write shares pages until a write, and refcounting writes on reads: every time a worker touches a shared object its count changes and its page is copied, and the cyclic GC's header writes do the same. Mitigate with gc.freeze() after loading (moves objects out of the GC's view, #29), keep the bulk data in non-object form (NumPy arrays, mmap, Arrow) so there are few Python objects to touch, and load per-worker data lazily. On 3.12, core objects are immortal. Watch per-worker unique set size (USS), not RSS.

Compare

Reference counting Cyclic GC (#29)
Frees anything whose count hits 0 unreachable cycles
When immediately, inline periodically, by allocation thresholds
Cost a write on almost every instruction pauses proportional to tracked objects
Deterministic yes, in CPython no
Can disable no yes (gc.disable())

Pitfalls

  • "del x deletes the object"
    It deletes a name and decrements the count.
    ↳ So: the object is freed only if that was the last reference; there's no way to destroy a referenced object.
  • "A function's locals are freed when it returns"
    Unless something still references its frame.
    ↳ Symptom: a stored exception keeps the traceback → frame → locals alive (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: store the message, or traceback.clear_frames.
  • "sys.getrefcount tells me how many variables hold an object"
    It counts every reference, plus one for its own argument.
    ↳ Also: on 3.12 it returns a fixed sentinel for immortal objects.
  • Not the same as the cyclic GC
    ↳ Difference: refcounting frees immediately at zero; the GC finds cycles that never reach zero, on its own schedule.
    ↳ So: gc.disable() turns off cycle collection only, never refcounting.
  • Don't rely on refcount-timed cleanup for files, sockets or locks.
    ↳ Why: it's a CPython detail: PyPy doesn't refcount, and an extra reference delays it indefinitely.
    ↳ Instead: with blocks and explicit close().
  • Don't keep exceptions, frames or tracebacks in long-lived structures.
    ↳ Why: each one pins every local of every frame it passed through.
    ↳ Instead: keep type(exc).__name__ and str(exc), or clear the frames first.
  • 🔖 Version: immortal objects since 3.12 (PEP 683); free-threaded 3.13+ uses split (biased) refcounts.
    ↳ So: refcount numbers differ across versions and builds; reason about +1/−1, not absolute values.

Connections

Path:object headerreference countingcyclic GCweakrefs
  • Builds on the object header: ob_refcnt is the counter in every box.
  • Used by the cyclic GC: it exists only for what refcounting can't free.
  • Contrasts with weak references: a reference that deliberately doesn't count.
  • Breaks when combined with threads and fork: unsynchronised counts need the GIL, and count writes un-share copy-on-write pages.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Swift's ARC and C++'s shared_ptr count references too; the JVM and Go use tracing collectors instead.

notes.title: The Cyclic Garbage Collector
notes.html:
References

gc: garbage collector interface · CPython InternalDocs: garbage collector design · 📜 PEP 442: Safe object finalization · rushter: Garbage collection in Python · GeeksforGeeks: Garbage collection in Python

TL;DR

Refcounting frees most garbage instantly; the cyclic GC exists only for objects that keep each other alive. It tracks containers in three generations and pauses in proportion to what it scans.

Flow:allocations pass a thresholdcollect a generationcopy each refcountsubtract references coming from inside the setanything still above 0 is reachable, along with all it reachesthe rest is a garbage cycle: finalize once, clear, freesurvivors move up a generation

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does the cyclic GC collect? Only unreachable reference cycles; refcounting handles the rest.
Which objects are tracked? Containers (lists, instances, frames); never ints or strs; some dicts and tuples untracked.
Draw by hand: a garbage cycle parent → children list → child → parent, no outside arrow: copy counts, subtract inside refs, all 0 → unreachable.
How does it find unreachable objects? Copy refcounts, subtract internal references; what's left at 0 is only referenced internally.
What does gc.freeze() do? Moves tracked objects to a permanent generation collections skip, for pre-fork servers.
Pause cost? Proportional to tracked objects scanned: ~24 ms for 1M instances (3.12).

The idea

A tree frees itself the moment you drop the root. Add one back-pointer, as every real tree, doubly linked list or ORM relationship does:

import gc
class Node:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name, self.children = name, []
    def __del__(self): print(f"  freed {self.name}")

gc.disable()                              # watch refcounting on its own
parent, child = Node("parent"), Node("child")
parent.children.append(child)
child.parent = parent                     # back-pointer: now it's a cycle
del parent, child
print("names deleted")                    # → names deleted   (nothing freed)
gc.collect()                              # → freed parent · freed child · returns 4

Both nodes are unreachable, but each still has a reference from the other, so neither count reaches zero. gc.collect() found them, plus the two children lists, and freed all four.

The trade: the cyclic GC reclaims what refcounting never can, paid for with periodic pauses whose length grows with the number of container objects the program keeps alive.

How it works

A collection finds objects referenced only from inside the set being scanned:

The rules around the algorithm (all measured on CPython 3.12):

Rule What actually happens
Only containers are tracked Only objects that can hold references can be in a cycle, so CPython tracks lists, dicts, instances, frames and closures via the GC header, never ints or strings. It also untracks containers that can't currently cycle: gc.is_tracked({"a": 1}) and gc.is_tracked((1, 2)) are False, gc.is_tracked([]) is True.
Three generations, triggered by allocations Thresholds (700, 10, 10): gen 0 runs at 700 net tracked allocations, gen 1 every 10 gen-0 runs, gen 2 also needs pending promotions above 25% of gen 2. 2 million short-lived allocations beside 1 million long-lived objects gave 1,832 gen-0, 166 gen-1 and zero gen-2 collections.
No roots needed; finalizers are safe Subtracting internal references (via each type's tp_traverse) leaves outside references, so no root set is needed (the picture). PEP 442 (3.4) runs __del__ once, checks for resurrection, clears weakrefs and calls tp_clear; refcounting then frees them. gc.garbage is almost always empty.
Pause cost is proportional to what's scanned A full gc.collect() took ~2 ms with 100,000 live instances and ~24 ms with 1,000,000; 300,000 garbage self-cycles took ~17.5 ms. Young collections are short and frequent; full ones rare but heap-sized.

Code

Where GC settings matter: a pre-fork server, following the gc.freeze() docs:

# gunicorn.conf.py
import gc

preload_app = True                     # load app, models, big dicts once, in the master
workers = 4
gc.disable()                           # no collections while the master builds the heap

def pre_fork(server, worker):
    gc.freeze()                        # inherited objects → permanent generation, never scanned

def post_fork(server, worker):
    gc.enable()                        # workers collect only objects they create
    gc.set_threshold(50_000, 20, 20)   # optional: measure p99 before and after, don't assume

A full collection in a child would write the GC header of every inherited object and copy every page it touches. On 3.12, freezing 1 million tracked objects took the next full collection from ~24 ms to effectively zero; refcount writes still un-share some pages (#28).

Break it: a bound method stored on self.

import gc, weakref
class Session:
    def __init__(self):
        self.buffer = bytearray(50_000_000)    # 50 MB of request state
        self.on_close = self.close             # bound method of self → a cycle
    def close(self): ...
gc.disable()
s = Session(); alive = weakref.ref(s); del s
print("after del:", alive() is not None)
gc.collect(); print("after collect:", alive() is not None); gc.enable()
# look for: True after del, so the 50 MB survived
# naive model predicts: freed on del, like any object with no names

On CPython 3.12.13 it prints after del: True, then after collect: False. One innocent attribute made a cycle; in production that shows as a memory sawtooth rather than a clean leak, and with the GC disabled it never drops.

Interview

30-second answer: CPython frees most objects by reference counting, the moment their count hits zero. That can't free cycles, where objects reference each other, so a separate generational collector tracks container objects in three generations, runs when allocations cross thresholds, and finds groups referenced only from inside themselves. Its pauses scale with the tracked objects it scans, which is why pre-fork servers use gc.freeze().

Q · Mechanism — How does the collector find unreachable cycles without knowing the program's roots? For the generations being collected, it copies each object's refcount into a scratch field, then walks every object's outgoing references and subtracts one from each target inside the set. What remains counts references from outside. Anything above zero is reachable, and so is everything it reaches; the rest is referenced only internally. It runs finalizers once (safe since PEP 442), re-checks for resurrection, clears weakrefs and calls tp_clear, and refcounting frees the objects.

Q · Failure — A service's memory rises in a sawtooth, and after someone set gc.disable() for latency it grows until OOM. Diagnose. The sawtooth is cycles accumulating between collections, typically per-request objects with back-references: parent links, bound methods stored on self, closures capturing their owner, exceptions holding frames. Disabling the GC removed the only thing freeing them. Find them with gc.collect() return counts, gc.set_debug(gc.DEBUG_SAVEALL) on a canary, or objgraph; break them with weakref back-pointers or explicit close(). If latency was the goal, gc.freeze() long-lived state and raise thresholds instead of disabling.

Q · Design — A latency-sensitive service holds millions of long-lived objects and shows periodic p99 spikes. How do you approach GC? First confirm it's the GC: gc.callbacks timing each collection, correlated with spikes. The binding constraint is pause cost proportional to tracked objects, so shrink what's tracked: gc.freeze() after startup, long-lived bulk data in NumPy, Arrow or __slots__ records, avoiding per-request cycles so young collections stay cheap. Then tune thresholds against measured p99 and CPU. Watch collection duration by generation alongside p99.

Compare

Lever What it changes Cost / risk
gc.freeze() inherited/startup objects never scanned frozen garbage is never collected
raise threshold0 fewer young collections larger pauses, more memory between runs
gc.disable() no cycle collection at all every cycle leaks
weakref back-pointers cycles never form must handle the referent disappearing
fewer tracked objects smaller pauses requires data-shape changes

Pitfalls

  • "Python's GC frees all memory"
    Refcounting frees almost everything; the GC only handles cycles.
    ↳ So: most memory problems are references you still hold, not the GC failing.
  • "gc.disable() is a safe latency optimisation"
    It stops cycle collection entirely.
    ↳ Symptom: every per-request cycle leaks until OOM.
    ↳ Instead: gc.freeze() long-lived state, or raise thresholds and measure.
  • "Objects with __del__ in a cycle are never collected"
    That was before PEP 442 (3.4).
    ↳ Now: finalizers run once and the cycle is collected; gc.garbage is almost always empty.
  • Not the same as reference counting
    ↳ Difference: refcounting is immediate and deterministic; the GC runs on thresholds and only frees unreachable cycles.
    ↳ So: gc.collect() returning 0 doesn't mean there's no leak.
  • Don't store bound methods of self on self, or parent pointers as strong references.
    ↳ Why: each creates a cycle that holds everything the object references until a collection (see Break it).
    ↳ Instead: weakref.WeakMethod, weakref.ref(parent), or look up the method when needed.
  • Don't tune thresholds without measuring.
    ↳ Why: higher thresholds mean fewer but larger pauses and more memory between runs.
    ↳ Instead: time collections with gc.callbacks against p99, before and after.
  • 🔖 Version: PEP 442 finalizers 3.4; gc.freeze() 3.7; default thresholds (700, 10, 10) on 3.12.
    ↳ Also: 3.14 made collection incremental (young + old generations), and the free-threaded build uses a non-generational collector, so re-measure pauses per version.

Connections

Path:reference countingcyclic GCweakrefs & finalizationdiagnosing memory
  • Builds on reference counting: it only handles what counts can never bring to zero.
  • Builds on the object header: tracked containers carry the 16-byte GC header.
  • Same mechanism as deepcopy: both traverse an object graph and must survive cycles.
  • Used by weak references: the usual way to avoid creating the cycle at all.
  • Same idea elsewhere: the JVM and Go use tracing collectors for everything; CPython traces only to clean up after refcounting.

notes.title: weakref & Finalization
notes.html:
References

weakref: weak references · weakref.finalize · Data model: __del__ · GeeksforGeeks: Weak references

TL;DR

A strong reference keeps an object alive; a weak reference finds it without adding to its refcount. For cleanup, weakref.finalize runs once and reliably; __del__ runs late, at shutdown, or swallows errors.

Flow:weakref.ref(obj) adds itself to obj's weakref list, refcount unchangedthe last strong reference goesrefcount 0just before dealloc, every weakref is cleared and its callback firesr() returns None, weak dict entries vanish, finalize cleanup runs

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does a weak reference do? Points at an object without incrementing its refcount; r() is None once it's gone.
Why does weakref.ref(obj.method) die at once? Bound methods are created per access; use weakref.WeakMethod.
finalize vs __del__? finalize runs once, can run early, runs at exit; __del__ timing and context are fragile.

The idea

A cache dict holds a strong reference to every value, so it decides their lifetime and grows forever without eviction. A weak dict remembers values only while something else keeps them alive:

import weakref
class Image:
    def __init__(self, key): self.key = key

cache = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()
img = Image("a"); cache["a"] = img
"a" in cache                     # → True    someone still uses it
del img
"a" in cache                     # → False   entry vanished on its own
weakref.ref([1, 2])              # → TypeError: cannot create weak reference to 'list' object

When the last strong reference went, refcounting freed the image and the weak entry disappeared:

Built-in int, str, tuple, list and dict can't be weakly referenced (their subclasses can), and neither can __slots__ classes without "__weakref__".

The trade: you can find an object without owning it, and you must handle it disappearing at any moment.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
Objects keep a list of their weakrefs An object that supports them has a slot (the __weakref__ attribute ordinary classes get) listing the weakrefs pointing at it. Creating one leaves the refcount unchanged (verified on CPython 3.12).
Death clears weakrefs and fires callbacks Just before deallocation CPython clears every weakref in the list and calls its callback: that's how WeakValueDictionary and WeakKeyDictionary drop dead entries and how finalize runs.
finalize is the reliable cleanup hook Doesn't keep the object alive, runs at most once, can be triggered early, and by default still runs at interpreter exit. Its callback must not reference the object, or the object could never die.
__del__ is fragile Runs whenever refcounting frees the object (any time, any thread), possibly at shutdown with module globals already None; its exceptions are printed and ignored. In cycles it runs only when the cyclic GC gets there.

Code

A registry that never extends lifetimes, and cleanup that doesn't depend on __del__:

import weakref

class Connection:
    _live = weakref.WeakValueDictionary()      # metrics registry: must not keep conns alive

    def __init__(self, dsn):
        self._sock = open_socket(dsn)
        Connection._live[id(self)] = self
        # runs on collection, at interpreter exit, or when close() calls it: exactly once.
        # It must not reference self, or self could never be collected.
        self._finalizer = weakref.finalize(self, close_socket, self._sock)

    def close(self):
        self._finalizer()                      # explicit close: runs now, never again

    @classmethod
    def live_count(cls):
        return len(cls._live)                  # only connections something else still holds

close() stays the primary path; the finalizer is the safety net for callers who forget.

Interview

30-second answer: A weak reference points at an object without increasing its refcount, so it doesn't keep it alive; calling it returns the object, or None once it's gone. WeakValueDictionary and WeakKeyDictionary build caches and registries on that, and entries vanish when the object dies. For cleanup I use weakref.finalize, which runs exactly once and at exit, instead of __del__, whose timing and shutdown behaviour are fragile.

Q · Mechanism — What happens to a weak reference when its object dies, and why is finalize more reliable than __del__? The object keeps a list of weakrefs to it. When its refcount reaches zero (or the GC frees it in a cycle), CPython clears each weakref so it returns None and calls each callback, which is how weak dicts drop entries. finalize is a registered callback of that kind: it holds the function and arguments but not the object, runs at most once, can be called early, and runs at exit by default. __del__ runs on whatever thread drops the last reference, possibly during shutdown, and swallows its exceptions.

Compare

dict WeakValueDictionary WeakKeyDictionary lru_cache
Keeps values alive yes no yes (values) yes
Keeps keys alive yes yes no yes
Entries vanish when never value dies key dies evicted by size
Use for owned data caches of shared objects per-object metadata bounded memoisation

Pitfalls

  • "A weak reference keeps the object around a bit longer"
    It adds nothing to the refcount.
    ↳ Symptom: weakref.ref(Image("tmp"))() is None immediately, because nothing else held it.
  • "__del__ is Python's destructor; put cleanup there"
    It runs late, on any thread, maybe at shutdown, and swallows exceptions.
    ↳ Instead: with/close(), plus weakref.finalize as the safety net.
  • "weakref.ref(obj.method) tracks the method"
    The bound method is created per access, so the weakref dies at once.
    ↳ Fix: weakref.WeakMethod(obj.method).
  • Not the same: WeakValueDictionary and WeakKeyDictionary
    ↳ Difference: the first lets values die (caches of shared objects); the second lets keys die (metadata attached to objects you don't own).
  • Don't reference the object from its own finalize callback.
    ↳ Why: the finalizer holds its arguments strongly, so the object can never be collected.
    ↳ Instead: pass only the resources (the socket, the path).
  • Don't iterate a weak dict while objects may die.
    ↳ Why: entries can disappear mid-iteration when another reference drops.
    ↳ Instead: iterate over list(d.items()), a snapshot.
  • 🔖 Version: WeakMethod and finalize are 3.4+.
    ↳ Note: timing of weakref callbacks follows refcounting on CPython; on PyPy they fire when the GC runs.

Connections

Path:reference countingcyclic GCweakrefs & finalization
  • Contrasts with reference counting: a weak reference is the one kind that doesn't count.
  • Used by caches and observer lists: WeakValueDictionary lets the owners, not the cache, decide lifetime.
  • Breaks when combined with slots: no __weakref__ slot, no weak references.
  • Contrasts with the cyclic GC: weak back-pointers prevent the cycle instead of collecting it later.
  • Same idea elsewhere: Java's WeakReference / WeakHashMap and Swift's weak var, the standard fix for retain cycles.

notes.title: Memory Allocators & Arenas
notes.html:
References

C API: memory management · rushter: Memory management in Python · GeeksforGeeks: Memory management in Python

TL;DR

Small objects (≤ 512 bytes) come from pymalloc: 1 MiB arenas → 16 KiB pools → fixed-size blocks. Freed blocks are reused by Python, and an arena goes back to the OS only when every block in it is free.

Flow:request ≤ 512 Bround up to one of 32 size classestake a free block from a 16 KiB pool of that classno pool free? carve one from a 1 MiB arenano arena? mmap a new onefree: block back to its poolarena returned only when every block in it is free

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which allocations does pymalloc handle? ≤ 512 bytes, in 32 size classes; larger ones go to system malloc.
Arena / pool sizes on 3.12? 1 MiB arenas, 16 KiB pools.
Why does RSS stay high after freeing most objects? A few survivors pin each arena, so none can return to the OS.

The idea

Free most of your objects, tracemalloc agrees they're gone, and RSS barely moves. It looks like a leak and usually isn't:

items = [{"i": i} for i in range(2_000_000)]    # RSS ~17 MB → ~464 MB
survivors = items[::50]                          # keep 2%, spread evenly
del items                                        # RSS stays ~464 MB
del survivors                                    # RSS drops to ~36 MB

(RSS from ps, CPython 3.12.13, macOS arm64.) Small objects aren't allocated from the OS one by one; CPython carves them from large arenas, and an arena can only go back when every object in it is free. One live object per arena pins them all.

The trade: small allocations are fast and cheap because pymalloc reuses its own memory, and memory returns to the OS only in whole, completely empty arenas.

How it works

Rule What actually happens
Three layers for small requests A request ≤ 512 B is rounded up to one of 32 size classes (16, 32, 48 … 512). pymalloc hands out a free block from a 16 KiB pool of that class, carves a new pool from a 1 MiB arena when needed, and mmaps a new arena when all are full; sys._debugmallocstats() reports this layout on 3.12.
Freeing is local; returning is all-or-nothing A freed block goes back on its pool's free list. An arena returns to the OS only when all its pools are empty (the picture), so scattered survivors keep RSS high while Python's own reuse works fine.
Large requests are the platform's business Above 512 B CPython calls the system malloc: on this macOS machine 300 MB of freed 1 MB bytearrays stayed in RSS, while glibc on Linux typically mmaps large blocks and unmaps them on free.
Free lists and alternatives Floats, small tuples and frames keep their own free lists on top. PYTHONMALLOC=malloc bypasses pymalloc (Valgrind, ASan need it); the free-threaded build (3.13+) uses mimalloc.

Code

Tell "Python is holding freed memory" apart from "something is still alive", inside a running worker:

import gc, os, re, sys, tempfile, tracemalloc

def memory_report() -> dict:
    gc.collect()                                     # rule out cyclic garbage first (#29)
    traced = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[0] if tracemalloc.is_tracing() else None
    with tempfile.TemporaryFile("w+") as f:          # stats go to the C-level stderr fd
        saved = os.dup(2); os.dup2(f.fileno(), 2)
        try:
            sys._debugmallocstats()
        finally:
            os.dup2(saved, 2); os.close(saved)
        f.seek(0); stats = f.read()
    arenas = int(re.search(r"arenas allocated current\s*=\s*(\d+)", stats).group(1))
    live = int(re.search(r"bytes in allocated blocks\s*=\s*([\d,]+)", stats).group(1).replace(",", ""))
    return {"traced_bytes": traced, "arenas_mb": arenas, "pymalloc_live_mb": live / 1e6}

Read it as a ratio. Arenas far above live blocks means fragmentation (on 3.12, a million small dicts with every fiftieth kept reported 218 arenas holding 6.8 MB). Both close and growing means real accumulation, so diff with tracemalloc (#32). RSS far above both means memory outside pymalloc: large blocks, C extensions, the platform allocator. _debugmallocstats is CPython-private, so its format can change.

Interview

30-second answer: CPython serves small allocations, up to 512 bytes, from its own allocator, pymalloc: 1 MiB arenas split into 16 KiB pools, each pool handing out blocks of one size class. Freed blocks are reused for new objects, but an arena only goes back to the OS when it's completely empty. So a process that frees most of its objects can keep its RSS if survivors are scattered, which looks like a leak but is fragmentation.

Q · Mechanism — Why might RSS stay flat after freeing 98% of a large structure, and how do you prove it's not a leak? The freed objects' blocks went back to pymalloc's pool free lists, but each 1 MiB arena still holds a few survivors, so none can be released. Python will reuse that memory for new small objects; the OS just doesn't get it back. Prove it with the ratio: tracemalloc and pymalloc's live-block bytes are small while arena count is high. A leak shows live bytes growing; fragmentation shows arenas high and live bytes flat.

Pitfalls

  • "RSS not dropping after del means a leak"
    Usually it's pymalloc keeping partly used arenas.
    ↳ Proof: tracemalloc and live-block bytes drop while arena count stays high.
    ↳ Leak instead: live bytes keep growing across requests.
  • "Freed memory goes back to the OS"
    Small-object memory returns only in whole empty arenas.
    ↳ Why: the allocator manages 1 MiB arenas, not individual objects.
  • Not the same: pymalloc and system malloc
    ↳ Difference: pymalloc serves ≤ 512 bytes with arena rules; larger requests follow the platform allocator, which may or may not return memory.
    ↳ So: big buffers and small objects behave differently after del.
  • Don't fight fragmentation with gc.collect() loops.
    ↳ Why: the GC frees cycles; it can't move survivors to compact arenas.
    ↳ Instead: allocate long-lived objects early and together, or recycle workers (max_requests).
  • Don't debug C-level memory errors with pymalloc on.
    ↳ Why: it hides individual allocations from Valgrind and ASan.
    ↳ Instead: run with PYTHONMALLOC=malloc.
  • 🔖 Version: 512-byte threshold, 16 KiB pools and 1 MiB arenas on 3.12; the free-threaded build (3.13+) uses mimalloc.
    ↳ Also: RSS figures here are macOS arm64; Linux behaves differently for large blocks.

Connections

Path:reference countingallocators & arenasdiagnosing memory
  • Builds on the object header: most boxes are small enough to live in pymalloc blocks.
  • Used by diagnosing memory: "arenas ≫ live blocks" is the fragmentation branch of its diagnosis flow.
  • Contrasts with reference counting: freeing an object is immediate; giving its memory back to the OS is not.
  • Contrasts with free-threaded CPython: mimalloc replaces pymalloc there.
  • Same idea elsewhere: size-class slab allocators like jemalloc and tcmalloc, and the JVM's TLABs inside a heap it rarely returns.

notes.title: Diagnosing Memory
notes.html:
References

tracemalloc · gc.get_referrers · Memray · objgraph · GeeksforGeeks: Diagnosing memory leaks

TL;DR

RSS is three layers: live Python objects, freed memory the allocator kept, and native memory. Diagnose by comparing layers: gc.collect(), then a tracemalloc diff, then allocator stats or Memray.

Flow:RSS grows under steady loadgc.collect() drops it? cycleselse tracemalloc diff over a traffic windowtraced total grows with RSS? a live reference, walk referrers to the rootarenas ≫ live blocks? fragmentationotherwise native memory: Memray

Recall

Prompt Answer
First step when RSS grows? gc.collect(): if memory drops, it was cyclic garbage.
What does a tracemalloc diff show? Net allocations retained between snapshots, grouped by line or traceback.
Traced flat, RSS rising? Not Python objects: allocator retention (#31) or native memory (Memray).
Who keeps an object alive? gc.get_referrers(obj) repeatedly, or objgraph's back-reference chain.
Draw by hand: the RSS triage gc.collect drops it → cycles · traced grows with RSS → live refs · arenas ≫ live → fragmentation · else native.

The idea

RSS climbs under steady load, and the usual move is to guess which structure grows. Ask the interpreter instead: snapshot, let traffic run, snapshot, diff.

import tracemalloc, leaky
tracemalloc.start()
for i in range(1_000): leaky.handle(i)            # warm up normal caches
before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for i in range(1_000, 21_000): leaky.handle(i)    # "an hour of traffic"
for stat in tracemalloc.take_snapshot().compare_to(before, "lineno")[:3]:
    print(stat)
# → leaky.py:4: size=3763 KiB (+3594 KiB), count=41902 (+40000), average=92 B
# → driver.py:6: size=625 KiB (+625 KiB), count=20000 (+20000), average=32 B
# → leaky.py:5: size=576 KiB (+540 KiB), count=1 (+0), average=576 KiB

(CPython 3.12.13.) Line 4, the payload dict, gained 40,000 blocks, two per request, none freed. The request-ID ints grew one per request because they're now dict keys. Line 5 is one allocation that keeps growing: the dict's own table resizing (#21). Growing count on one line plus one growing table on the next is the signature of an unbounded cache.

The trade: tracemalloc turns memory growth into a ranked list of source lines, at the cost of slowing every allocation while on and seeing only memory allocated through Python.

How it works

Diagnosis is a triage; each step removes one explanation:

Rule What actually happens
How tracemalloc sees allocations It hooks CPython's PyMem_*/PyObject_* allocators, captures the Python traceback (nframes, default 1) per block and drops it on free. compare_to groups two snapshots by "lineno", "filename" or "traceback" and ranks the differences.
What it costs An allocation-heavy loop ran ~5× slower with one frame and ~29× with 25 (CPython 3.12); get_tracemalloc_memory() reports its own overhead. Trace shallow, on one canary, for a bounded window.
What it can't see Only Python's allocators: a C extension's malloc and memory the allocator kept are invisible (the picture's yellow and red layers). A block is credited to its first allocation, so free-list reuse keeps the old trace (see Break it).
From "which line" to "who holds it" A diff says where growing objects were allocated; gc.get_referrers(obj), walked back to a global, class attribute, closure or traceback, says what keeps them alive (reference counting). objgraph draws the chain.

Code

An opt-in diagnostic for one canary worker, logging the top growing lines:

import gc, logging, os, threading, tracemalloc

log = logging.getLogger("memdiag")
NOISE = [tracemalloc.Filter(False, tracemalloc.__file__),
         tracemalloc.Filter(False, "<frozen importlib._bootstrap*>")]

def start_memory_diagnostics(interval_s=600, top=10):
    if os.environ.get("MEMDIAG") != "1":                       # opt-in: one canary, not the fleet
        return
    tracemalloc.start(int(os.environ.get("MEMDIAG_FRAMES", "1")))   # 1 frame: ~5x, not ~29x
    baseline = tracemalloc.take_snapshot().filter_traces(NOISE)
    def loop():
        while True:
            threading.Event().wait(interval_s)
            gc.collect()                                       # don't blame cycles on a line
            snap = tracemalloc.take_snapshot().filter_traces(NOISE)
            for stat in snap.compare_to(baseline, "lineno")[:top]:   # vs baseline: slow growth shows
                log.warning("memdiag %s", stat)
    threading.Thread(target=loop, name="memdiag", daemon=True).start()

Raise MEMDIAG_FRAMES only once you know the line and need its callers.

Break it: two handlers allocate every call; only one keeps what it allocates.

import gc, tracemalloc
kept = {}
def leaky(i):  kept[i] = {"id": i, "body": "x" * 200}     # retained
def churny(i): tmp = f"{i}:" * 50                         # freed on return
tracemalloc.start(); gc.collect(); before = tracemalloc.take_snapshot()
for i in range(20_000): leaky(i); churny(i)
gc.collect()
for stat in tracemalloc.take_snapshot().compare_to(before, "lineno")[:3]: print(stat)
# look for: leaky's line tops the diff; churny's line is absent
# naive model predicts: both lines, since both allocate on every call

On CPython 3.12.13 leaky's line tops it at about +4 MiB and +40,001 blocks, the loop line follows (the int keys kept now holds), and churny isn't there: diffs report net retained memory, not allocation volume. A trap found writing this: if churny builds a dict, the diff blames churny, because leaky reuses dicts from the free list that still carry churny's trace.

Interview

30-second answer: I separate three layers RSS mixes together. First gc.collect(): if memory drops, it was cyclic garbage. Then a tracemalloc snapshot diff over a window of traffic, which ranks the source lines whose allocations are being retained; then gc.get_referrers or objgraph to find what holds them. If traced memory is flat while RSS rises, it's allocator retention or native memory, and I switch to allocator stats or Memray.

Q · Mechanism — How does tracemalloc attribute memory to a line, and what are its blind spots? It hooks Python's allocator functions; every allocation records the current traceback, up to nframes, against the block's address, and frees remove it. A snapshot copies the table; compare_to groups by line and ranks net change. Blind spots: native allocations from C extensions, memory pymalloc kept after a free, and first-allocation attribution, so free-list reuse can blame a neighbouring line. It also costs ~5–29× on allocation-heavy code, so it runs on a canary.

Q · Failure — Workers OOM after about a day; memory climbs linearly with requests. Walk through the investigation. Linear with requests means something is retained per request. Confirm with gc.collect(): no drop, so not cycles. Enable tracemalloc with one frame on one worker, diff against a baseline after an hour: the top line shows the allocation site (typically a module-level cache, a list of errors holding tracebacks, or a registry). Take a sample object and walk gc.get_referrers to the root. Fix the ownership (bound it, weakref it, clear frames), add a canary alert on RSS slope, and keep worker recycling as a backstop, not the fix.

Q · Design — Design memory observability for a fleet of Python services so leaks are caught before they OOM. Always on and cheap: per-worker RSS and USS, RSS slope per request, GC collection counts and durations via gc.callbacks, and an alert on sustained slope rather than absolute size. On demand and expensive: tracemalloc on one canary behind a flag, Memray for native suspicion, snapshot diffs shipped as logs. Containment: worker recycling (max_requests) and memory limits with headroom. Watch RSS slope per request first: flat means healthy, linear means a retained reference.

Compare

Tool Sees Cost Use for
RSS / USS (ps, cgroups) everything, no attribution ~0 detecting growth
gc.collect() + counts cyclic garbage a pause ruling cycles in or out
tracemalloc Python allocations by line ~5–29× on alloc-heavy code finding the allocation site
gc.get_referrers / objgraph who holds an object slow, ad hoc finding the root
Memray Python + native allocations heavier, run on demand C extensions, allocator retention

Pitfalls

  • "sys.getsizeof on the suspicious structure will tell me the leak size"
    It's shallow, and you don't know which structure yet.
    ↳ Instead: a tracemalloc diff ranks retained memory by allocation site.
  • "If tracemalloc shows nothing, there's no leak"
    It only sees Python's allocators.
    ↳ So: traced flat with RSS rising means fragmentation or native memory: check allocator stats, then Memray.
  • "The line a diff blames is the line that leaks"
    It's where the block was first allocated.
    ↳ Trap: free-list reuse can blame a neighbouring line that makes temporaries of the same type (see Break it).
    ↳ Fix: confirm with gc.get_referrers on a sample object.
  • Not the same: allocation site and retainer
    ↳ Difference: tracemalloc says where objects were made; referrers say what keeps them alive.
    ↳ So: fixing the allocation line rarely fixes a leak; removing the retaining reference does.
  • Don't run tracemalloc across the whole fleet by default.
    ↳ Why: it slows allocation-heavy code ~5× to ~29× and adds memory per live block.
    ↳ Instead: one canary, one frame, a bounded window.
  • Don't treat worker recycling as the fix.
    ↳ Why: max_requests hides the growth and resets your evidence before you find the cause.
    ↳ Instead: keep it as a backstop and fix the retained reference.
  • 🔖 Version: numbers here are CPython 3.12.13; free-list behaviour and allocator internals vary by version.
    ↳ Also: tracemalloc has been in the stdlib since 3.4; Memray is a third-party tool (Linux and macOS).

Connections

Path:reference countingcyclic GCallocatorsdiagnosing memory
  • Builds on all four notes before it: each branch of the triage is one of them, and the diagnosis flow is this note's own mechanism.
  • Used by reference counting: "who holds it?" is a walk back along references.
  • Used by lru_cache and module-level dicts: the most common unbounded caches a diff points at.
  • Contrasts with profiling CPU: memory growth is about retention over time, so you diff two snapshots rather than sample one run.
  • Same idea elsewhere: heap dumps compared in Java's Eclipse MAT or VisualVM, and Go's pprof heap diff.
